Research Update

Tunable coordinate-network bank with off-mesh quadrature · viscous Burgers 2D and 3D

23 October 2026

Three parts: the r dial, mesh independence of cost and iterations, and accuracy against speed in 2D and 3D. Accuracy numbers are against the order-verified references on development and validation cases; the sealed test cases are still closed.

Part 1

The dial and the mesh

One trained bank; choose how many shapes to use; the solve does not depend on the mesh.

Question

Do iterations or decoding depend on the mesh?

Iterations are flat; only writing the output grows

  • Solve: r 128 ≈ 22 ms, r 256 ≈ 52 ms, r 384 ≈ 88 ms at every mesh
  • Iterations: 51.5–54.3 Levenberg–Marquardt iterations per 50 steps, same on every mesh; at most 5 in any step
  • Decode: 0.13–0.18 ms at 256² → 5.7–14.3 ms at 4096²
  • Solid BE, dashed CN-R: schemes overlap

P1 timing job 5352971 (H200), frozen test modes, 6 dev cases × 3 repeats; Codex-checked · 5

Iteration counts are Levenberg–Marquardt trial iterations per time step summed over the run (rejected trials included; a step can need 0 if the predictor is already converged). Each step also builds one Jacobian before iterating, so Jacobian builds = 50 + iterations ≈ 104 per run ≈ 2.1 per step at r = 384. Mesh flatness is shown for r = 128–384; r = 512 was timed only at 1024². the solver never sees the mesh after the initial fit, so they cannot change with it. Decode is the six output fields on the full mesh, which is the only mesh-dependent part.

make_rotation.py; P1 analysis.json, 16-case subset (figs/make_error_vs_r_fig.py) · 3

Question

How do we get a dial r from one network?

Reorder the 512 shapes so the first r are the best r

  • QR of the shapes on a grid makes them orthonormal
  • SVD of all training coefficients sorts directions by how much they are used
  • Result: one rotation T; the first r columns are the best r-shape model
  • Median error (CN-R, 16 cases): r 128 → 0.69 %, 256 → 0.27 %, 384 → 0.25 %, 512 → 0.24 %; flat after 256 (the time step takes over)
This is what makes the bank tunable: smaller r is cheaper, larger r is more accurate, and no retraining is needed. 3D captures 99.97 % of coefficient energy with 128 shapes.

Question

How many quadrature points does the nonlinear term need?

Gauss and Fibonacci rules pass with a few thousand points; Sobol and Smolyak need far more

  • ρ: worst relative error of the quadrature nonlinear term against a converged reference (Gauss 640²), over every state the model reaches
  • Acceptance bar: ρ ≤ 0.116
  • At about 4,000 points: Gauss 0.019, Fibonacci 0.033
  • Sobol converges slowly; Smolyak (a control) never reaches the bar
  • The old 63² mesh lattice (triangle) is measured against its own mesh target, so it is not directly comparable

Off-mesh quadrature study 2D, accurate setting, 1024², dev+val · 5

This is the off-mesh quadrature of the nonlinear term u·∇u: the network and its exact derivative are evaluated at m fixed points in the unit square, the same on every mesh. Gauss and Fibonacci lattices converge fast because the integrand is smooth; random-like Sobol points converge roughly as one over root m. The number of points grows with the bank width: about 4,000 at r = 128 up to about 37,000 at r = 512, and that is what drives the cost per step.

Question

What do the quadrature points cost, and does that depend on the mesh?

Cost grows with the number of points, never with the mesh

  • Accurate: r = 384, 1536 tests; fast: r = 128, 512 tests
  • Every rule is flat from 256² to 4096²: ratio 0.94–1.06 over all 40 measured arms
  • More points cost more: Gauss 64² (4,096) → 96² (9,216) → 128² (16,384) → Fibonacci 17,711
  • At 4096²: Gauss 96² 54.5 ms against the old 63² lattice 46.3 ms (accurate); Fibonacci 1597 13.3 ms against 18.7 ms (fast)

Off-mesh quadrature study 2D, one H200 job, dev6 × 3 repeats; solve = query − decode · 6

Solve time is the median query time minus the median decode time, on one GPU, so it is the reduced-space work only. The old 63-by-63 mesh lattice (dashed) is on the mesh, so it is not a matched equal-accuracy comparison; the off-mesh rules are measured against the continuum and the lattice against the mesh. In the accurate setting the off-mesh rule needed to pass the quadrature check (Gauss 96²) costs a little more than the old lattice; in the fast setting Fibonacci 1597 is cheaper.

Part 2

Accuracy against speed

How our model compares with full solvers and with tuned POD reduced models, in 2D and 3D.

Question

In 2D, how cheaply do full solvers reach our accuracy?

A coarse spectral solver reaches our accuracy band at far lower cost

  • Grey band: the accuracy our LSPG models reach at 1024² (median and worst)
  • Green: sine pseudo-spectral with ETDRK4 reaches that band at the lowest cost
  • Orange (central + CN-R) and blue (upwind + BE) need much more time
  • Example at 4096²: our r = 384 CN-R query 97 ms against 11.7 ms for the matched spectral solver

jcp-fom2d; why-spectral report · 8

Each curve is the cheapest tested member of a full-solver family at each accuracy level, timed on an H200. Smooth Burgers in a box needs only a handful of sine modes, which is why the spectral family wins.

Question

In 2D, what is our speed-up at matched accuracy?

Slower

Below 1× for every configuration, closing as the mesh grows

  • Speed-up S = full-solver cost ÷ our cost at the same accuracy; above 1 means we are faster
  • At 4096²: S = 0.049–0.71 across 21 configurations; none reaches the 2× bar
  • S rises with the mesh because our solve cost is flat while the full solver's grows
  • Smaller r (blue, r = 128) is closest to break-even

jcp-fom2d; final report §3.4 · 9

Every S is an upper bound on our speed-up, because the full-solver ladder is finite. Kill criterion K2 (no 2× win at the largest mesh) fires.

Question

In 2D, how do we compare with a tuned POD reduced model?

Slower

POD with ECSW or Q-DEIM matches our accuracy in less time

  • Red stars: our qualified configurations; dots: POD + ECSW (blue), Q-DEIM (orange), none (grey)
  • Dominated (faster and more accurate) in 8 of 8 configurations at 256² and at 1024²
  • Example: ours r = 384 CN-R 86.8 ms, worst 1.78 %; POD + ECSW 30.7 ms, worst 1.35 %

jcp-hr-baselines; final report §3.5 · 10

Same timing job for both, so the comparison is like for like. Developmental, in-sample, unadjusted evidence. POD snapshots came from the best full solver on the target mesh.

Question

In 3D, does the accuracy–cost dial work?

Works

Yes: wider banks buy accuracy, and the qualified model is 2.95× faster than our earlier one

  • Each dot is a numerically qualified 3D configuration (bank width, quadrature, solver)
  • The black front: the cheapest configuration at each accuracy level
  • Qualified speed-up 2.95× over our earlier wide model C_W768 at comparable accuracy
  • Earlier unqualified claims (5.4×, 17×) are withdrawn

jcp-dims H2q; final report (H2q row) · 11

Cost is relative to C_old, so this is ROM against ROM, not against full solvers. Mesh-path query at 65³ on an H200.

Question

In 3D, how do we compare with full solvers and POD?

Slower

Both are faster: the full solver by 6–130×, POD in most cells

  • Against the best matched full solver at 384³: S = 0.0079–0.16 (4 models)
  • Against POD at 65³: dominated in 5 of 5 (diagnostic batch) and 2 of 4 (qualified batch)
  • POD here failed its own basis-adequacy check, so its results carry that restriction

jcp-speed3d; jcp-hr-baselines; final report §3.4–3.5 · 12

6–130× is the inverse of S = 0.158 to 0.0079. Developmental, in-sample; ECSW coverage incomplete in 3D.

Question

All together: where do we stand against the best full solver?

Every configuration sits left of 1×; 3D is furthest behind

  • Blue: 2D at 1024²; orange: 2D at 4096²; green: 3D at 384³
  • Dashed line: break-even (1×); solid: the 2× bar we registered
  • 2D gets closer at the bigger mesh; 3D stays at 0.008–0.16

final report §3.4 (union of full-solver families) · 13

The union means the fastest full solver of any family that reaches the same accuracy. These verdicts are on development and validation cases.

Question

Newest: does a faster time stepper change the picture?

New

With ETDRK4 the bank beats the tuned spectral solver by up to 2×, but so does POD

  • Purple (our bank + ETDRK4): S = 0.81–2.07, above 1 in most cells
  • Red (our bank, standard LSPG): S = 0.044–0.40
  • Blue/orange (POD-Galerkin, POD + ECSW): up to 2.14 and 2.01, about the same as ours
  • Best on narrow families (W = 0.08); falls as the family widens

imp-box (E1) final report, audited; box, H200, val32 · 14

Provisional: errors are against the lane's own spectral references, many points sit at the cheapest model the search tried, and several cells were deferred for budget. ETDRK4 failed the worst-error rule in the 1024² fast-step lane, so it must be qualified here before we claim it.

Question

What does this add up to?

Mesh-independent and tunable; not yet faster than the best alternatives

ComparisonWhereResult
Mesh independence of cost and iterations2D and 3DYes: flat within 1.01–1.09
Accuracy dial r2D 128→512; 3DImproves to r ≈ 256–384, then flat
Against the best full solver (deployed LSPG)2D 4096²; 3D 384³Slower: S 0.049–0.71; 0.0079–0.16

Bank + ETDRK4 on the box (new)2D box, narrow to wide1–2× over spectral; level with POD (provisional)

final report; jcp-dims; imp-box · 15

The open lever is the time integrator: the deployed LSPG step costs about two Jacobian builds and the decode grows with the mesh. With ETDRK4 the bank reaches parity with POD on the box, which is the strongest result so far, pending qualification.

RESEARCH UPDATE · BURGERS 3D REFINEMENT

Time refinement improves the median and worsens outliers

On the fixed diagnostic cases, median error falls from 4.075% to 2.079%, while worst error rises from 4.379% to 5.59%.

Both endpoints pass the subset convergence checks. More frequent matrix refresh does not make physical error uniformly smaller.

The coarse and fine endpoints were selected after these diagnostics, before the full-validation sweep. The intermediate setting remains a valid measured tradeoff.

Error cancellation is a hypothesis. The inherited bank uses analytic advection and grid-dependent diffusion; it does not share POD's discrete residual.
